related_questions.question: How long does immigration keep records?

text_blocks.snippet: Immigration records, specifically an individual's "A-File", are generally kept permanently by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). After 100 years from the individual's birth date, these files are transferred to the National Archives and Records Administration, where they are kept indefinitely. Other immigration records, like receipts, may have specific retention periods, but the core file is retained long-term.
snippet_highlighted_words: generally kept permanently by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

list.title: A-Files:
list.snippet: These files, containing an individual's entire immigration history, are stored by DHS for 100 years after the individual's birth. After that, they are transferred to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) for permanent storage.

list.title: Other Records:
list.snippet: Certain records, like those related to specific applications or forms, may have shorter retention periods. For example, Form I-9, used to verify an employee's identity and authorization to work, must be kept for 3 years after the date of hire or 1 year after termination, whichever is later.

list.title: Digital Records:
list.snippet: In the digital age, immigration agencies like USCIS have the capacity to store and access files more easily. This contributes to the long-term retention of immigration records.

list.title: Freedom of Information Act (FOIA):
list.snippet: Individuals can request their own immigration records or, with permission, someone else's, through FOIA. This includes A-Files and other relevant documentation.

list.title: National Archives:
list.snippet: The National Archives also holds immigration records, particularly for arrivals between 1820 and December 1982. They also digitize records and make them available through partners' websites.
